title: Transitivity I: 自動詞/他動詞 — が vs を

grammarPoints.rule: Japanese verbs come in two kinds. Some describe something HAPPENING — the door opens. Others describe somebody DOING it — I open the door. English uses "open" for both; Japanese uses two verbs. あく is the door opening, あける is you opening it. They are not two forms of one word — they are separate entries about the same event from two sides, the way English has "rise" and "raise". And the particle in front always tells you which: the happening verb takes が, the doing verb takes を. ドアが あく。 ドアを あける。

examples.ja: ドアが あく。
ドアを あける。
まどが あく。
まどを あける。
ミカが ドアを あける。

antiPattern.why: あく is the door opening by itself, so nobody is doing anything to it and を has no job — が is the only particle it takes: ドアが あく。

grammarPoints.rule: The second pair, same shape: しまる is the door closing, しめる is you closing it. There is nothing to memorise about which is which — you read it off the sentence. Find the noun in front of the verb and look at its particle. が means it happened. を means somebody did it. It works in both directions: given 「まどが しまる」 you know nobody closed it, and to say "I closed the window" you know you need を, and therefore しめる. Learners who struggle with pairs are trying to FEEL the difference. Do not feel it. Read the particle.

examples.ja: ドアが しまる。
ドアを しめる。
まどが しまる。
まどを しめる。
ミカが まどを しめる。

antiPattern.why: しめる needs somebody doing the closing, and が says nobody is — either say 「まどが しまる」 (it closes) or 「まどを しめる」 (I close it).

grammarPoints.rule: The third pair, and the last one you get half of free. はいる you have had since module 16 — 「へやに はいる」, I go into the room. いれる is the other side of it, putting a thing in: 「かばんに ほんを いれる」. Watch what the particles do. With はいる the thing that moves takes が, and where it goes takes に. With いれる the thing that moves takes を, because somebody is moving it, and where it goes still takes に. The に never changes. Only the が/を slot does, and it changes because a doer arrived.

examples.ja: かばんに ほんを いれる。
examples.en: I put a book in my bag.

examples.ja: へやに はいる。
かばんに かぎが はいる。
examples.en: The key goes in the bag.

examples.ja: ミカが かばんに さいふを いれる。
examples.en: Mika puts her wallet in her bag.

examples.ja: へやに おおきい つくえが はいる。
examples.en: A big desk goes in the room.

antiPattern.ja: かばんに ほんが いれる。
antiPattern.why: いれる needs somebody doing the putting, and が does not supply one — the book being put takes を: かばんに ほんを いれる。

grammarPoints.rule: Here is the payoff — the piece module 14 could not finish. ている has two readings: an action still running (たべている, is eating) and a state left behind by a change (しっている, knows). Module 14 could not say WHICH verbs do which, because the answer is what you just learned. A 自動詞 + ている is almost always the second kind: the change already happened, and you are describing how the thing is NOW. 「ドアが あいている」 is not a door in the act of opening — it is a door that is open. Same with 「まどが しまっている」: the window is shut.

examples.ja: ドアが あいている。
まどが しまっている。
ドアが あいて いるから、さむい。
examples.en: The door is open, so it's cold.

examples.ja: きょうしつの まどが あいている。
みせが しまっている。

antiPattern.ja: ドアを あけている。
antiPattern.why: that IS good Japanese, but it means somebody is in the middle of opening the door — the を-verb keeps its doer. For the STATE of a door that is already open you need the が-verb: ドアが あいている。

grammarPoints.rule: Two pairs about stopping, both half-owned already. とまる you met last module — 「でんしゃが とまる」, the train comes to a halt. Its partner とめる is what a driver does: 「くるまを とめる」, I stop the car. Same が/を tell, no new machinery. Worth noticing: the pair is asymmetric in real life. Trains stop by themselves constantly and cars almost never do, so とまる turns up with trains and machines, とめる with cars and people. That is not a rule to learn — it falls out of what the verbs mean.

examples.ja: でんしゃが とまる。
くるまを とめる。
きかいが とまる。
みせの まえに くるまを とめる。
examples.en: I park the car in front of the shop.

examples.ja: バスが えきに とまる。
examples.en: The bus stops at the station.

antiPattern.ja: でんしゃを とまる。
antiPattern.why: とまる is the train stopping on its own, so it takes が — 「でんしゃが とまる」. を would need a doer, and for that you want とめる, which is what the driver does.

grammarPoints.rule: きめる you have owned since module 30: I decide. Its partner きまる has no clean English word — it means the thing got decided, without saying by whom. 「じかんが きまる」 is "the time is settled". Japanese reaches for this constantly where English would use a passive, and it is your first look at a habit that runs through the language: when who-did-it is not the point, Japanese puts no doer in the sentence at all. It just uses the が-verb.

examples.ja: じかんが きまる。
じかんを きめる。
りょこうが きまる。
ミカが みせを きめる。
あした テストの じかんが きまる。
examples.en: The time of the test will be settled tomorrow.

antiPattern.why: きまる is the time settling with nobody named, so it takes が — if you want to say YOU settled it, the verb is きめる: じかんを きめる。

grammarPoints.rule: The last taught pair, and the first where BOTH halves are new — the honest test of whether the rule has landed, because there is no familiar half to lean on. けす is what you do: 「でんきを けす」, turn the light off. きえる is what happens: 「でんきが きえる」, the light goes out. English changes the whole phrase — "turn off" versus "go out" — and Japanese changes only the verb and the particle. けす also covers a screen and a sound, so 「テレビを けす」 and 「おとを けす」 are both ordinary.

examples.ja: でんきを けす。
でんきが きえる。
テレビを けす。
きょうしつの でんきが きえる。
ミカが テレビを けす。

antiPattern.why: きえる is the light going out on its own and takes が. If somebody is switching it off, the verb is けす: でんきを けす。

grammarPoints.rule: Three more pairs, and this time you are not being taught a rule — you already have it. You are being shown where else it turns up. はじまる / はじめる: it starts / I start it. でる / だす: it comes out / I take it out. おちる / おとす: it falls / I drop it. Read each against its particle and every one behaves exactly like あく / あける. That is the point of meeting them together and quickly: nine pairs in, the pattern should be doing the work, not your memory. You will use all three again next module.

examples.ja: えいがが はじまる。
えいがを はじめる。
でんしゃが でる。
かばんから ほんを だす。
examples.en: I take a book out of my bag.

examples.ja: さいふが おちる。

antiPattern.ja: えいがを はじまる。
antiPattern.why: はじまる is the film starting on its own — が. The を-verb is はじめる, which needs somebody to start it: えいがを はじめる。

to be decided, to be settled
to turn off, to switch off
to go out, to go off (of a light)
to begin something, to start something
to take out, to put out
to drop something, to let something fall
